coverage_note: Authority proposal for Bahrain MOTC. Leads with the domestic archipelago network (built on the Kingdom's existing water-taxi corridors); cross-Gulf links to Qatar and Saudi Eastern Province are secondary and optional.

partner_context.their_ambition: Bahrain MOTC is modernizing public transport across land, sea, and air — the planned Bahrain Metro, an upgraded bus network, and, since April 2025, the Kingdom's first water taxi. The ambition is a connected, low-emission network that uses Bahrain's island geography as an advantage.
partner_context.their_pressure: Road and causeway corridors are congested at peak, the Kingdom is committed to net-zero by 2060 and a 30% emissions cut by 2035, and waterfront communities keep growing faster than roads can serve them.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the vessel upgrade that lets the water-transport mode Bahrain has already launched scale into a real network: faster, near-silent, zero-emission foiling boats that run in more weather and reach the whole archipelago — integrated with the bus network, the planned Metro, and the Masar app.

hero.title: A national water-transport network for Bahrain
hero.subtitle: Bahrain already put water taxis on the map. Navier is the zero-emission, foiling upgrade that turns them into a fast, all-weather network across the whole archipelago — and a credible relief valve for the causeway at peak.

why_now: Bahrain is an archipelago — Manama, Muharraq, Amwaj, Diyar, Reef Island, Sitra and the outer islands all face the same sheltered water, yet most trips between them still loop along congested causeways and coast roads. In April 2025 the Kingdom launched its first water taxi across six stations in Manama and Muharraq, proving people will choose the water when it is faster. Navier builds on that head start: a near-silent, low-wake, zero-emission foiling service that is quicker than today's boats, runs in more conditions, and can reach islands and corridors the current fleet cannot.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling is a genuine step-change in speed, comfort, wake, and noise over conventional small craft — enough to make scheduled water transport a serious everyday mode, not a sightseeing novelty.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: The first routes use what already exists: the six live water-taxi stations, the Kingdom's marinas and jetties, and airport and resort arrivals. No new roads, bridges, or land take are needed to start.
why_navier_now.the_moment: The water taxi is live, the Bahrain Metro is in preparation, and a direct Bahrain–Qatar passenger ferry opened in November 2025. Water transport is already part of the Kingdom's plan — this is the moment to make it fast, clean, and archipelago-wide.
wow_corridors: Manama ↔ Muharraq inner-harbour shuttle (the live water-taxi corridor, upgraded)
Manama ↔ Amwaj and Diyar island network
Manama Corniche ↔ Bahrain International Airport jetty
Manama ↔ Sitra and Durrat Al Bahrain along the east coast
Cross-Gulf links to Qatar and Saudi Eastern Province (optional, later)

multimodal_fit: The water layer is national transport infrastructure, not a ride-hail add-on. It plugs into the bus network and the planned Bahrain Metro at shared interchanges, shares ticketing through the Masar app the Kingdom already uses for the water taxi and the Qatar ferry, and gives the airport a direct waterside arrival. Every route adds capacity to the public network without adding a single car to the causeways.

journeys_unlocked.with_navier: The live water-taxi corridor, foiling-upgraded — quicker, quieter, and running in more weather.

differentiation.headline: Built for public value
differentiation.body: This proposal is measured the way an authority measures transport: trips shifted off congested roads and causeways, emissions avoided against the 2035 and 2060 targets, island and airport access widened, and waterfront districts and tourism better served. It is a public network with a credible operating model — not a marketplace.

proof_points.claim: Bahrain launched its first water taxi in April 2025, with six stations across Manama and Muharraq — water is already public transport here.
proof_points.evidence: Masar Group Water Taxi Project (air-conditioned vessels, ~28 pax, Masar app booking).

proof_points.claim: A direct Bahrain–Qatar passenger ferry opened in November 2025 (Sa'ada Marina ↔ Al-Ruwais, 70–80 minutes) — the first direct sea route in the Gulf.
proof_points.evidence: Launched 6 November 2025, booking via the Masar app.

proof_points.claim: The King Fahd Causeway carries roughly 33 million crossings a year and is congested at peak — a marine relief corridor addresses real demand.
proof_points.evidence: Causeway crossing volumes; congestion at peak periods.

proof_points.claim: Bahrain targets net-zero by 2060 with a 30% emissions cut by 2035; a zero-emission marine mode contributes directly.
proof_points.evidence: National carbon-neutrality commitments under Bahrain Economic Vision 2030.

objections.q: Is this proven, or a novelty?
objections.a: Bahrain already runs a water taxi and a Qatar ferry. Navier is the foiling upgrade to a mode the Kingdom has already chosen — faster, cleaner, and able to run in more weather.
No. The first routes use the six existing water-taxi stations and the Kingdom's marinas, jetties, and airport arrivals. The network grows from what is already built.

objections.q: How does it fit the rest of public transport?
objections.a: It connects to the bus network and the planned Metro at shared interchanges and shares ticketing through the Masar app. It adds capacity without adding cars to the causeways.
Around public value — emissions avoided, congestion relieved, access widened — plus a transparent operating model. The exact fares, frequencies, and cost-recovery are set with the authority.

phases.narrative: A full archipelago network links every major waterfront community across sheltered domestic water, widening access without building a single new road.

phases.narrative: Bahrain's mid-Gulf position makes it a natural regional hub, but the case stands on its domestic network first; cross-Gulf links are an option for later, not the headline.

use_cases.label: regional travel

use_cases.label: causeway relief
use_cases.summary: Divert peak causeway demand onto a fast, clean marine alternative.

the_ask: Partner with Navier on a feasibility study: upgrade the existing water-taxi corridors with zero-emission foiling vessels, map the full archipelago network with the authority, and scope an optional cross-Gulf relief pilot — all integrated with the Masar app and the wider public-transport plan.
close: Bahrain has already shown its people will choose the water. Navier turns that head start into a fast, clean, national network — domestic archipelago first, cross-Gulf links when the Kingdom is ready.

end_state.headline: A national water-transport network for Bahrain: the live water-taxi corridors upgraded to zero-emission foiling, a full archipelago network across the islands, and optional cross-Gulf links to Qatar and Saudi Eastern Province.
